questions.title: Settling spheres and model limits
questions.stem: A solid sphere of radius $1.00\,\mathrm{mm}$ and density $3000\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$ falls through a stationary liquid of density $1000\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$ and dynamic viscosity $0.200\,\mathrm{Pa\,s}$. Use $g=9.81\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. For slow laminar motion, drag magnitude is $6\pi\eta rv$.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the three forces on the sphere and show that the net downward driving force, excluding drag, is $\tfrac43\pi r^3(\rho_s-\rho_l)g$.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the terminal speed in this model.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Predict the terminal-speed change if the radius is doubled while all other quantities remain fixed.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: State one reason your prediction in (c) might fail for a sufficiently large sphere.

steps.text: Weight acts down; buoyancy and motion-opposing viscous drag act up.
Weight is $\tfrac43\pi r^3\rho_s g$ and buoyancy is the displaced-liquid weight $\tfrac43\pi r^3\rho_l g$.
Subtracting yields $F_{\rm drive}=\tfrac43\pi r^3(\rho_s-\rho_l)g$.
At terminal speed, $6\pi\eta rv_t=F_{\rm drive}$, so $v_t=2r^2(\rho_s-\rho_l)g/(9\eta)$.
With the other parameters fixed, the model gives $v_t\propto r^2$.
Doubling radius makes the speed four times as large, $0.0872\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
For example, flow may cease to be laminar so Stokes drag no longer applies, or the sphere may become too large for container-wall effects to be negligible. Accept a specific relevant limitation.

questions.answerSummary: (a) Subtracting yields $F_{\rm drive}=\tfrac43\pi r^3(\rho_s-\rho_l)g$.; (b) $v_t=0.0218\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.; (c) Doubling radius makes the speed four times as large, $0.0872\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.; (d) For example, flow may cease to be laminar so Stokes drag no longer applies, or the sphere may become too large for container-wall effects to be negligible. Accept a specific relevant limitation.

questions.title: A lamp and a cell with internal resistance
questions.subtopic: A lamp and a cell with internal resistance
questions.stem: A cell of emf $12.0\,\mathrm V$ and internal resistance $1.00\,\Omega$ is connected in series with a $2.00\,\Omega$ resistor and a filament lamp. The lamp characteristic is shown and is described by $V_L=I^2$, with $V_L$ in volts and $I$ in amperes. Use the positive operating current.

sourceAnchors.focus: Circuit loop and branch reasoning, changed to a nonlinear lamp operating point

questions.changeNotes: Rebuilt context/data and part sequence with independently recomputed results and a new precise figure where useful.
questions.cognitiveDemand: Link physical models, interpret conditions and justify the result.

verification.notes: See the named reproducible author checks and worked solution for this question.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain why the lamp does not obey Ohm's law over this range.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Derive the circuit load-line relation between $V_L$ and $I$.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the operating current, graphically or by calculation.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Calculate the fraction of the cell's electrical power dissipated in the lamp.

steps.text: $V_L/I=I$ varies with current, so the characteristic does not have constant resistance.
Apply the loop rule including both the external $2.00\,\Omega$ and internal $1.00\,\Omega$ resistances.
Intersect the load line with the lamp curve, or solve $I^2+3I-12=0$.
$I=(-3+\sqrt{57})/2=2.27\,\mathrm A$. Accept a reasonable graphical value, approximately $2.2$ to $2.35\,\mathrm A$.
Lamp power is $P_L=IV_L$; total cell power supplied is $\varepsilon I$.
The fraction is $V_L/\varepsilon=I^2/12.0$.
The fraction is $0.431$, approximately $43.1\%$. Use unrounded current, or follow through a reasonable graphical value.

questions.answerSummary: (a) $V_L/I=I$ varies with current, so the characteristic does not have constant resistance.; (b) $12.0=V_L+3.00I$, so $V_L=12.0-3.00I$.; (c) $I=(-3+\sqrt{57})/2=2.27\,\mathrm A$. Accept a reasonable graphical value, approximately $2.2$ to $2.35\,\mathrm A$.; (d) The fraction is $0.431$, approximately $43.1\%$. Use unrounded current, or follow through a reasonable graphical value.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe the displacement node and antinode positions in the fundamental mode.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the fundamental frequency.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the next allowed resonance frequency.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The measured fundamental is $98.6\,\mathrm{Hz}$. Infer the end correction, assuming $L_{\rm effective}=L_{\rm physical}+e$.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: State the pressure-oscillation condition at the closed end.

steps.text: The closed end is a displacement node because the fluid cannot move through it.
The open end is approximately a displacement antinode; the fundamental fits one-quarter wavelength in the effective length.
$\lambda_1=4L$, so $f_1=v/(4L)$.
Only odd harmonics are allowed, so the next resonance is $3f_1=303\,\mathrm{Hz}$.
$L_{\rm effective}=343/(4\times98.6)=0.8697\,\mathrm m$.
$e=0.8697-0.850=0.0197\,\mathrm m$, approximately $2.0\,\mathrm{cm}$.
The closed end is a pressure antinode (maximum pressure-variation amplitude).

questions.answerSummary: (a) The open end is approximately a displacement antinode; the fundamental fits one-quarter wavelength in the effective length.; (b) $f_1=343/(4\times0.850)=101\,\mathrm{Hz}$.; (c) Only odd harmonics are allowed, so the next resonance is $3f_1=303\,\mathrm{Hz}$.; (d) $e=0.8697-0.850=0.0197\,\mathrm m$, approximately $2.0\,\mathrm{cm}$.; (e) The closed end is a pressure antinode (maximum pressure-variation amplitude).

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain why the globally averaged absorbed intensity is $(1-\alpha)S/4$.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the equilibrium temperature.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: The albedo falls to $0.250$ while emissivity remains fixed. Determine the new equilibrium temperature.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Give two limitations of this model when used for a real planet.

steps.text: The planet intercepts sunlight over projected area $\pi R^2$ but distributes/radiates it over surface area $4\pi R^2$.
Only fraction $1-\alpha$ is absorbed, giving global average $(1-\alpha)S/4$.
At equilibrium $(1-\alpha)S/4=\varepsilon\sigma T^4$.
$T=244\,\mathrm K$ to three significant figures.
$T_{\rm new}=254\,\mathrm K$ to three significant figures. Retain unrounded values.
For example, real temperatures differ with latitude, day/night and seasons, so one uniform $T$ need not represent emission exactly.

For example, clouds/atmospheric absorption and emission cannot generally be represented by one fixed emissivity; albedo and emissivity may change with temperature. Award two distinct relevant limitations, not duplicate wording.

questions.answerSummary: (a) Only fraction $1-\alpha$ is absorbed, giving global average $(1-\alpha)S/4$.; (b) $T=244\,\mathrm K$ to three significant figures.; (c) $T_{\rm new}=254\,\mathrm K$ to three significant figures. Retain unrounded values.; (d) For example, clouds/atmospheric absorption and emission cannot generally be represented by one fixed emissivity; albedo and emissivity may change with temperature. Award two distinct relevant limitations, not duplicate wording.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain how the neutron chain reaction can be kept approximately steady.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the thermal power produced by fission.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Convert the energy released per fission into joules.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Determine the fission rate.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Determine the mass of uranium-235 nuclei undergoing fission per day.

parts.label: f
parts.prompt: Explain why the mass-equivalent of the released energy is much smaller than the mass calculated in (e).

steps.text: On average, each fission must lead to one subsequent fission; too many or too few surviving fission-producing neutrons change the rate.
Neutron-absorbing control rods regulate neutron survival; in a thermal reactor a moderator slows neutrons to increase the likelihood of further fission.
$P_{\rm thermal}=640\,\mathrm{MW}/0.400=1.60\times10^9\,\mathrm W$.
$\dot N=P_{\rm thermal}/E_f$.
$m=1.69\,\mathrm{kg}$ of uranium-235 nuclei per day. This is not the total mass of fuel assemblies.
Almost all initial mass remains in fission fragments and emitted particles; only the small difference in total rest mass is converted to released energy.

questions.answerSummary: (a) Neutron-absorbing control rods regulate neutron survival; in a thermal reactor a moderator slows neutrons to increase the likelihood of further fission.; (b) $P_{\rm thermal}=640\,\mathrm{MW}/0.400=1.60\times10^9\,\mathrm W$.; (c) $E_f=200\times10^6\times1.60\times10^{-19}=3.20\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm J$.; (d) $\dot N=5.00\times10^{19}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.; (e) $m=1.69\,\mathrm{kg}$ of uranium-235 nuclei per day. This is not the total mass of fuel assemblies.; (f) Almost all initial mass remains in fission fragments and emitted particles; only the small difference in total rest mass is converted to released energy.
